MSK–SKIN · GROSS ANATOMY · LECTURE COMPANION

Gluteal Region & Posterior Thigh

Anatomy learned through landmarks, movement, neurovascular relationships, injury mechanisms and practical image recognition.

ObjectivesLO 1LO 2LO 3LO 4LO 5Master before moving onFirst Aid links

Learning objectives

  1. Identify os coxae and femoral landmarks, ligaments, surface projections and palpation points necessary for posture and gait.
  2. Identify gluteal muscles and explain pelvic stabilization, superior gluteal injury, and Trendelenburg gait.
  3. Trace structures through greater and lesser sciatic foramina using piriformis as the reference.
  4. Identify posterior thigh muscles, hamstring injuries and ischial avulsion; map popliteal boundaries, contents and pulse.
  5. Recognize gluteal and posterior-thigh structures on radiographs, MRI and CT.

Big picture

The hip links a stable pelvis to a mobile lower limb. Gluteus maximus supplies forceful hip extension; gluteus medius and minimus prevent pelvic collapse during single-leg support; deep rotators orient the femoral head; and hamstrings couple hip extension to knee flexion. The piriformis acts as an anatomical gatekeeper for vessels and nerves leaving the pelvis. Distally, those structures converge behind the knee in the popliteal fossa.

Bone + ligament landmarks → sciatic gateways → muscles and nerve supply → movement and gait → injury and imaging
LO 1

Bony landmarks, ligaments & sciatic spaces

Os coxae: orient the hip bone before memorizing labels

The innominate bone comprises ilium, ischium and pubis, which converge at the acetabulum. The lunate surface articulates with the femoral head; the acetabular fossa is the central nonarticular depression. On the medial ilium, find the auricular surface for sacroiliac articulation. Lateral gluteal lines mark muscle attachment territories.

LandmarkWhy it matters
ASIS / AIISASIS is palpable anteriorly and anchors tensor fasciae latae; AIIS is inferior to it.
PSIS / PIISPosterior orientation; PIIS contributes to the upper border of the greater sciatic notch.
Ischial spineAttachment for sacrospinous ligament; divides the greater and lesser sciatic notches.
Ischial tuberosityWeight-bearing prominence in sitting and attachment of major hamstring tendons.
Greater / lesser sciatic notchesBecome the sciatic foramina once bridged by sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments.
Pubic tubercle and ramiOrient the anterior and inferior portions of the pelvic ring.

Femur: posterior attachments explain muscular actions

At the proximal femur, distinguish the head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters; the intertrochanteric line is anterior and the intertrochanteric crest is posterior. The trochanteric fossa receives deep lateral rotator tendons; the quadrate tubercle anchors quadratus femoris. The gluteal tuberosity anchors deep gluteus maximus fibers; the linea aspera gives origin to short-head biceps femoris.

Ligaments convert notches into exits

Sacrospinous ligament runs from sacrum/coccyx toward the ischial spine. Sacrotuberous ligament extends toward the ischial tuberosity. Together they enclose the greater and lesser sciatic foramina, defining routes from the pelvis into the gluteal region and from gluteal region toward perineum.

MUST KNOW
Sacrospinous → ischial spine; sacrotuberous → ischial tuberosity. These two structures convert both sciatic notches into foramina.
A tendon avulses bone from the “sit bone.” Which landmark and muscle group should you immediately consider?
The ischial tuberosity; it is the common proximal attachment for the true hamstrings (and the long head of biceps femoris).
LO 2

Gluteal muscles, mechanics & Trendelenburg gait

First understand the movements

Hip extension moves the femur posteriorly relative to pelvis; abduction pulls it laterally; medial/lateral rotation turns the femur around its long axis. During single-leg stance the swing-side pelvis tends to fall, so stance-side abductors must counteract that drop. At the knee, flexion occurs in the sagittal plane; when flexed, hamstrings also rotate the leg.

Gluteal layers: power, stabilization and rotation

MuscleAttachments (lecture)Action / functionInnervation
Gluteus maximusIlium, sacrum, coccyx, sacrotuberous ligament → iliotibial tract and gluteal tuberosityHip extension, lateral rotation; rising from sittingInferior gluteal (L5–S2)
Gluteus mediusLateral ilium between anterior and posterior gluteal lines → greater trochanterAbduction, medial rotation; keeps pelvis levelSuperior gluteal (L4–S1)
Gluteus minimusLateral ilium between anterior and inferior gluteal lines → greater trochanterAbduction, medial rotation; keeps pelvis levelSuperior gluteal (L4–S1)
Tensor fasciae lataeASIS/anterior iliac crest → iliotibial tract → Gerdy’s tubercleTenses fascia lata, hip flexion; assists abduction/internal rotation; stabilizes extended kneeSuperior gluteal (L4–S1)

Trendelenburg: the stance leg tells the story

Superior gluteal nerve injured → weak medius/minimus on the stance side → insufficient contralateral pelvic stabilization → pelvis drops on the unsupported opposite side.

On a single-leg-stance test, a positive Trendelenburg sign is contralateral pelvic drop. Patients may lean the trunk toward the affected stance side to decrease the external moment at the hip. Contrast inferior gluteal injury: weakness of forceful hip extension, such as climbing stairs or rising from a chair.

COMMON CONFUSION
The pelvis falls opposite the weak stance-side abductors. For example, right superior gluteal nerve injury → pelvic drop on the left when standing on the right leg.

IT tract, lateral hip pain, and rotators

The iliotibial tract is a lateral thickening of fascia lata and a shared aponeurotic pathway for gluteus maximus and tensor fasciae latae. It terminates at the lateral proximal tibia (Gerdy’s tubercle). The slide specifically asks whether the IT band can be stretched and presents research that does not show a significant change in measured stiffness following the studied interventions; avoid promising that foam rolling permanently lengthens this dense fascial band.

EXAM TRAP
The lecture explicitly says: spell out “iliotibial” on the practical; do not rely on “IT” alone. IT band syndrome presents with lateral knee pain in repetitive flexion–extension, around an impingement zone near 30° knee flexion.

Greater trochanteric pain syndrome is typically lateral hip pain, worse lying on the affected side or prolonged standing. Slides emphasize gluteus medius/minimus tendinopathy rather than automatically assuming bursitis (80% without bursitis in the slide’s cited cohort). Snapping hip may be external (IT band or gluteus maximus over greater trochanter), internal (iliopsoas), or intra-articular.

Deep external rotators are piriformis, superior gemellus, obturator internus, inferior gemellus and quadratus femoris; the lecture notes the “deep six” also includes obturator externus. They rotate and stabilize the femoral head.

RotatorInnervation
PiriformisNerve to piriformis
Superior gemellus / obturator internusNerve to obturator internus (L5–S2)
Inferior gemellus / quadratus femorisNerve to quadratus femoris (L4–S1)
Obturator externusObturator nerve (anatomy handout)
During right single-leg stance the left pelvis sags. Which nerve and muscles are weak?
The right superior gluteal nerve and right gluteus medius/minimus. The dropping side (left) is not the injured side.
An athlete has lateral hip pain when lying on that side. Is bursitis necessarily the primary pathology?
No. The lecture emphasizes gluteal medius/minimus tendinopathy as the commonest component of greater trochanteric pain syndrome.
LO 3

Sacral plexus, gluteal gateways & neurovasculature

Piriformis is the map legend

Piriformis exits via the greater sciatic foramen. Identify its superior and inferior margins first: the superior gluteal nerve and vessels travel above, while most other major gluteal neurovascular structures travel below.

RouteStructures / important destination
Greater sciatic foramen, above piriformisSuperior gluteal nerve (L4–S1) and artery → between medius and minimus.
Greater sciatic foramen, below piriformisInferior gluteal nerve (L5–S2) and vessels; sciatic nerve (L4–S3); posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh (S1–S3); nerves to obturator internus and quadratus femoris; pudendal nerve (S2–S4) and internal pudendal vessels.
Greater sciatic foramen → around ischial spine/sacrospinous ligament → lesser sciatic foramenPudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels turn into perineum; nerve to obturator internus also re-enters through lesser foramen.
Lesser sciatic foramenAlso conveys the tendon of obturator internus exiting the pelvic wall toward greater trochanter.

Sacral plexus and distal consequences

The sacral plexus combines the lumbosacral trunk (L4–L5) and S1–S4. The massive sciatic nerve comprises tibial and common fibular components and normally passes inferior to piriformis. Tibial division largely innervates posterior thigh; the common fibular division is distinctive in the short head of biceps femoris.

The posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh supplies skin of lower buttock, posterior thigh and popliteal region. Cutaneous innervation over buttock also arises from cluneal nerves: superior (posterior rami L1–L3), middle (posterior rami S1–S3), inferior (branches of posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh, S2–S3). Their purely sensory role is important when distinguishing motor injuries.

Clinical application: avoid injuring the sciatic nerve

The slides show an intramuscular injection method targeting the superolateral gluteal region by palpating ASIS and iliac crest, selecting muscle away from major inferiorly directed gluteal nerves and the sciatic nerve. In practice, exact injection technique should follow current institutional guidance; the anatomical principle is to avoid the inferomedial buttock and vulnerable neurovascular bundles.

Deep gluteal syndrome refers to nondiscogenic sciatic nerve entrapment in the subgluteal space. Fibrous bands, piriformis, gemelli-obturator internus complex, quadratus femoris/ischiofemoral structures or hamstring pathology may provoke buttock/posterior thigh pain and sciatica-like symptoms. Hip rotation in flexion with knee extension may exacerbate symptoms.

CLINICAL CONNECTION
Sciatica-like pain does not prove a spinal disc lesion. Compression below piriformis can produce sciatic distribution symptoms from a deep gluteal source.
Which neurovascular bundle is the exception to the “inferior to piriformis” rule?
The superior gluteal nerve and artery pass superior to piriformis via the greater sciatic foramen.
A nerve leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, hooks around the ischial spine, then enters the perineum. What nerve?
The pudendal nerve (S2–S4); internal pudendal vessels travel the same route.
LO 4

Posterior thigh, hamstring injuries & popliteal fossa

Posterior compartment: one muscle group, two joints

Most hamstrings span the hip and knee: their posterior course allows hip extension plus knee flexion. The short head of biceps femoris is the exception because it arises from the femoral linea aspera, so it cannot extend the hip. In a flexed knee, medial hamstrings rotate the leg medially; biceps femoris rotates it laterally.

MuscleProximal → distalActionsInnervation
SemitendinosusIschial tuberosity → superior medial tibia, pes anserinusHip extension, knee flexion, medial leg rotationTibial division of sciatic
SemimembranosusIschial tuberosity → medial tibial condyleHip extension, knee flexion, medial leg rotationTibial division of sciatic
Biceps femoris long headIschial tuberosity → fibular headHip extension; knee flexion; lateral leg rotationTibial division of sciatic
Biceps femoris short headLinea aspera → fibular headKnee flexion; lateral leg rotation; no hip extensionCommon fibular division of sciatic

Mechanism predicts hamstring injury location

In rapid limb deceleration, eccentric loading can disrupt the myotendinous junction, frequently long-head biceps femoris. In excessive lengthening when the hip flexes as the knee extends, the lecture highlights proximal semimembranosus tendon. A severe proximal injury may tear tendon from ischial tuberosity in adults; in a skeletally immature patient, the weaker ischial apophysis may avulse a bone fragment.

LECTURE → STEP 1 BRIDGE
Hip flexion + knee extension → hamstring lengthening → injury near proximal attachment; in the adolescent → apophyseal avulsion rather than adult-style tendon tear.

Popliteal fossa: trace borders into contents

Think of a diamond behind the knee. Superolateral border: biceps femoris; superomedial: semitendinosus and semimembranosus; inferolateral: lateral gastrocnemius head; inferomedial: medial gastrocnemius head. Floor includes distal femur, posterior capsule/oblique popliteal ligament, and popliteus; roof is fascia and skin.

Within the fossa, the structures are arranged superficial to deep: tibial nerve → popliteal vein → popliteal artery (N–V–A). The common fibular nerve follows the lateral biceps femoris border. The small saphenous vein drains into the popliteal vein. Cutaneous sural branches are also displayed in the slides. The popliteal artery continues from the femoral artery and divides into anterior and posterior tibial arteries.

Pulse, genicular routes and aneurysm

Flex the knee to relax the roof, press deeply in the inferior popliteal fossa to detect the popliteal arterial pulse. A faint/absent pulse can suggest proximal arterial obstruction, but should be interpreted clinically. Four named genicular branches shown are superior medial, superior lateral, inferior medial and inferior lateral, which contribute to an anastomotic network around the knee.

A popliteal aneurysm can present as posterior knee swelling or pain and compromise distal perfusion. The lecture discusses genicular collateral circulation in relation to popliteal artery ligation; this is an anatomic collateral principle, not a recommendation to delay urgent vascular evaluation.

Which popliteal structure is deepest? Why is its pulse hard to palpate?
The popliteal artery is deepest (nerve → vein → artery superficial to deep); it lies against the floor of the fossa.
A teenage athlete has sudden proximal posterior thigh pain and a bone fragment at the ischial tuberosity. Explain the age-specific injury.
An ischial apophyseal avulsion fracture produced by strong traction at the hamstring origin.
LO 5

Radiographic, CT & MRI recognition

Use the same three-pass recognition approach in every image

  1. Orient: left versus right, axial/coronal/sagittal and modality.
  2. Anchor: identify bony structures (acetabulum, greater trochanter, ischial tuberosity, femur) and the prominent muscle compartments.
  3. Trace: find tendons, nerves and vessels relative to the landmarks; recognize abnormal fluid signal or displaced fragment when present.

Image-to-anatomy recognition list

View / focusFind without labelsPredict from anatomy
AP pelvic or hip radiographIliac crests, ASIS region, acetabulum, femoral head and neck, greater trochanter, ischial tuberositiesDisplaced fragment at ischial tuberosity in younger patient → hamstring-origin avulsion
Coronal hip MRIGluteus medius/minimus approaching greater trochanterLateral peritrochanteric changes → consider gluteal tendon pathology
Axial buttock / hip MRIGluteus maximus superficial, deeper lateral rotators, femoral head and trochanterSciatic pathway inferior to piriformis; recognize the deep gluteal compartment
Posterior thigh MRILong-head biceps femoris lateral; semitendinosus/semimembranosus medialEdema at myotendinous junction versus proximal tendon/attachment
PRACTICAL IMAGE
The original professor slides above are retained so the exact orientation, labels, arrows and highlighted abnormalities remain available for recognition practice. For higher-resolution reference, consult the corresponding original slide or assigned atlas plate.
On MRI, why might pathology next to the greater trochanter represent gluteal disease rather than isolated bursitis?
Gluteus medius/minimus insert on the greater trochanter; the lecture emphasizes tendon pathology as a common cause of lateral hip pain.

Master these before moving on

  1. Pelvic stability in single-leg stance. Stance-side superior gluteal-innervated abductors prevent contralateral pelvic drop; critical for gait analysis.
  2. Piriformis and the foramina. Locate piriformis before sorting superior versus inferior exiting bundles and structures looping into the lesser foramen.
  3. Hamstring exceptions. Short-head biceps femoris originates on femur and uses common fibular innervation; its function differs from true biarticular hamstrings.
  4. Fossa spatial arrangement. Boundaries predict where nerves, vein and deep artery lie; needed for clinical palpation, injury and imaging.
  5. Age and injury mechanism. Tendon rupture in adults versus apophyseal bone avulsion in a growing skeleton.

The most useful First Aid connections

The following are selective board-style extensions, not substituted for course instruction.

  1. FIRST AID CONNECTION: Superior gluteal nerve injury → Trendelenburg pelvic drop; distinguish from inferior gluteal nerve injury → difficulty with forceful hip extension.
  2. FIRST AID CONNECTION: Sciatic nerve anatomy helps localize deficits in tibial versus common fibular distributions; the short head of biceps femoris is a key exception.
  3. FIRST AID CONNECTION: Pudendal nerve roots S2–S4 and its exit/re-entry course are a classic anatomic localization clue.
  4. FIRST AID CONNECTION: Popliteal artery is deep to the vein and tibial nerve, contextualizing vascular injury and pulse examination.
